definition.text: A bias in which people's choices change with the way the same options are worded, even when the options are logically identical.

facts.text: When choices are worded as gains, most people prefer a sure gain to a chance of gain; worded as losses, people tend to pick a gamble over a sure loss.
In Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 disease problem, a sure treatment was chosen by 72% when described as saving 200 lives, but 78% chose the risky one when outcomes were described as deaths.
Standard logic says a decision should not depend on how the problem is described; deciding on such irrelevant wording is called an extensionality violation.
93% of PhD students registered early when a late penalty fee was stressed, but only 67% when the same terms were shown as an early discount.
Framing shapes decisions in public health, education, politics, law and economics, and is counted among the largest biases in decision making.
People are more open to framing when they rely on fast, intuitive thinking rather than slow, deliberate thinking.
The effect seems to weaken when a decision is made in a foreign language, perhaps because it brings more distance and deliberation.
Valuation surveys of environmental goods have been criticised for bringing in framing effects.

definition.text: Mental shortcuts people use to reach judgments and decisions quickly.

facts.text: Humans, animals, organizations and even machines use simple strategies to form judgments and solve complex problems fast.
Heuristic answers are good enough for a pressing need when information is incomplete, but they are not always right and can differ from what logic and probability give.
Herbert A. Simon introduced the idea in the 1950s, and his satisficing rule was one of the first models of a heuristic.
In the 1970s Tversky and Kahneman linked heuristics to cognitive bias, first proposing availability, representativeness, and anchoring and adjustment.
Theories differ on whether heuristics are irrational: one view treats them as unavoidable shortcuts for a limited brain, another as fast methods that do as well as complex ones with less information.
In a computer test of ten simple decision rules, most picked the option with the highest expected value and almost never the lowest.

definition.text: Judging how likely something is by how closely it resembles a typical member of a category.

facts.text: It attends to an individual's traits while ignoring how common each category is in the population, which leads to the base rate fallacy.
Asked about a woman named Linda, people rated 'bank teller and active feminist' as likelier than 'bank teller', though a combination can never be more probable than one part of it.
Tversky and Kahneman argued it underlies the gambler's fallacy, the expectation that random outcomes even out over the short run.

definition.text: An unnoticed mental process in which a hard question is answered by replacing it with an easier, related one.

facts.text: Daniel Kahneman and Shane Frederick proposed it in 2002.
It explains why people can be unaware of their own biases and why biases persist even after people are told about them.
In the bat-and-ball puzzle many people wrongly answer $0.10, splitting $1.10 into a big and a small amount instead of working out the sum.
Travellers paid more for insurance against death in a terrorist attack than for insurance covering death of any kind, as fear stood in for a judgment of total risk.

definition.text: The view, argued by Gerd Gigerenzer and colleagues, that simple rules of thumb can give judgments as accurate as complicated procedures.

facts.text: This approach holds that heuristics perform as well as complex methods, but faster and with less information.
A fast-and-frugal tree makes a classification, such as whether chest pain signals a heart attack, by asking a short sequence of questions on few cues.
Some theories argue that a heuristic can be more accurate than weighing every known factor, the so-called less-is-more effect.

definition.text: The tendency to keep putting resources into a failing course of action in the hope of turning losses around.

facts.text: It arises when organisations or nations must decide whether to continue an operation or withdraw from it.
It is especially likely when the decision maker can claim credit for success while others absorb the losses.
